events.title: 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre
events.subtitle: The people, the violence, and the lives behind the headlines
events.intro: From September 22 to 24, 1906, white mobs attacked Black Atlantans, killing residents and destroying businesses. False and sensationalized newspaper reporting, racial resentment, and political tensions helped fuel the violence. This archive follows individuals connected to South-View Cemetery: people killed in the attacks, and a business leader whose livelihood was targeted. Their lives deserve to be understood beyond the massacre itself.

sources.name: D. L. Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 5–6 (uploaded research book)

events.title: Atlanta Child Murders
events.subtitle: Remembering children and the communities that demanded answers
events.intro: Between 1979 and 1981, a series of killings of Black children, teenagers, and young adults left Atlanta families grieving and searching for answers. This section distinguishes the documented lives of victims from the broader work of community advocates. Research on specific South-View burials is ongoing; no individual is presented as a victim without verification.

sources.name: Smithsonian Institution Archives — International Year of the Child

events.title: Civil Rights Movement
events.subtitle: Leadership, voting rights, and the pursuit of equality
events.intro: Atlanta was a central city in the struggle for civil rights. The lives remembered at South-View reveal how organizing, education, faith, and public service helped reshape the city and nation.

sources.name: City of Atlanta — Promised Land cemetery tour

alonzoherndon.name: Alonzo Herndon
alonzoherndon.intro: Alonzo Herndon was a barber and entrepreneur who built the company that became Atlanta Life Insurance. His work supported Black economic independence, employment, and community institutions. Begin with that fuller life before entering the events that shaped it.

chapters.title: Freedom was a beginning.
chapters.text: Herndon was emancipated as a child in Georgia at the end of the Civil War. Juneteenth commemorates freedom’s announcement in Texas that year. His life connects directly to emancipation, while the Texas document shown here gives broader context; it does not place him in Galveston.

chapters.title: A livelihood in the path of violence.
chapters.text: During the Atlanta Race Massacre, white mobs smashed the windows of Herndon’s Peachtree Street barbershop. He had already gone home. The photograph shows the shop in 1903, before the attack: a place of work and ambition within a city facing racial violence.

alonzoherndon.legacy: Herndon’s story continues through business and family. His wife Adrienne was an educator, and their son Norris carried on the insurance enterprise. He deserves to be remembered for what he built as well as what his business endured.
alonzoherndon.note: Historical-context profile, not a massacre victim. Henderson, South-View (2018), p. 5, confirms his South-View burial.

georgeunionwilder.name: George Union Wilder
georgeunionwilder.role: Civil War veteran and 1906 massacre victim
georgeunionwilder.intro: George Union Wilder escaped slavery during the Civil War, served in the United States Army, and adopted “Union” as his middle name in recognition of his service. Decades later, he was killed during the Atlanta Race Massacre. His grave at South-View preserves an unusually direct historical record of the violence.

chapters.title: A life ended by racial violence
chapters.text: Wilder was killed in Brownsville during the September 1906 attacks. His grave marker commemorates both his Civil War service and his death in the massacre. Historical accounts do not establish every circumstance of his death.

georgeunionwilder.legacy: Wilder should be remembered not only for how he died, but also for his escape from slavery and his service in the Civil War.
georgeunionwilder.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View (2018), p. 5, confirms George Wilder was a Union soldier killed in the 1906 violence and buried at South-View.

franksmith.name: Frank Smith
franksmith.intro: Frank Smith worked as a messenger for Western Union. His ordinary working day became part of Atlanta’s tragic history when he was attacked during the violence of September 1906.

chapters.title: A messenger caught in the violence
chapters.text: Smith was attacked by a white mob near the Forsyth Street bridge. His death is documented in accounts of the massacre.

chapters.title: A name preserved
chapters.text: D. L. Henderson identifies Frank Smith as a telegraph office messenger killed by white rioters and buried in South-View’s historic section (South-View, p. 5).

franksmith.legacy: Smith’s work as a messenger connects the massacre to the everyday labor and mobility of Black Atlantans. Surviving accounts tell us more about his death than his family or aspirations; those details should not be invented.
franksmith.note: Burial documented by Henderson, p. 5; further details should be checked against original records.

marshallcarter.name: Marshall Carter
marshallcarter.intro: Marshall Carter was a young Black Atlantan whose life was cut short during the September 1906 violence. His story centers the children and families affected by the massacre.

chapters.title: A child’s life interrupted
chapters.text: Research associated with the 1906 massacre remembrance project identifies Carter as a 13-year-old schoolboy who died during the attacks.

chapters.title: Recovering a name
chapters.text: Historical death-certificate research has helped recover Carter’s identity and reported South-View burial. An individual cemetery record has not been independently reproduced in this student project.

marshallcarter.legacy: Remembering Carter means recognizing a child whose future was taken. More information about his family, school, and daily life would require additional archival investigation.
marshallcarter.note: South-View burial reported in massacre research; direct cemetery register not independently inspected.

stinsonferguson.name: Stinson Ferguson
stinsonferguson.intro: Stinson Ferguson was a young Black resident of Atlanta killed during the 1906 violence. The surviving record is fragmentary, making careful research especially important.

chapters.title: A life lost
chapters.text: Research on the massacre identifies Ferguson, approximately 25 years old, as a victim who died of a gunshot wound.

chapters.title: Following the paper trail
chapters.text: Death-certificate research links Ferguson to the massacre and reports a South-View burial. Further personal history and original burial documentation remain to be examined.

stinsonferguson.legacy: Ferguson’s name helps tell the story of the people behind the death toll. Rather than assign him undocumented accomplishments, this profile preserves the known details and identifies the gaps.
stinsonferguson.note: Burial reported in massacre research; original register entry not independently inspected.

annieshepard.name: Annie Shepard
annieshepard.intro: Annie Shepard, whose surname also appears as Sheppard or Shepherd in historical references, worked as a laundress. She was killed during the Atlanta Race Massacre.

chapters.title: A working woman’s story
chapters.text: Shepard’s occupation reminds us that the violence affected working people whose labor sustained Atlanta households and neighborhoods.

chapters.title: A burial recovered in historical records
chapters.text: A PBS documentary discusses Shepard’s burial in an unmarked area of South-View and shows researchers examining historical cemetery records. This profile relies on that documentary account rather than a personally inspected register entry.

annieshepard.legacy: Shepard should be remembered as a person and worker, not only a victim. The spelling variations and unmarked burial also show why archival research matters.
annieshepard.note: South-View burial supported by the PBS documentary discussed in project research; original register entry not independently inspected.
